source.title: Augmenting Visual Anomaly Detection with Automated Interpretability
source.authors: Antonio De Santis; Arsenio Leo; Marco Brambilla

record.tranche_reason: The study uses SAEs to decompose and edit anomaly residuals for visual anomaly detection. It does not test whether superposition occurs or its geometry, capacity account, or prevalence in language models.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses superposition in related work and uses SAE features as an intervention interface. Its main AUROC results evaluate an anomaly-detection method, not the superposition claims, so those results are not rows. RQ3 does report effects of individual SAE feature interventions; those bear on feature actionability but do not measure any listed version, so they are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The study uses TopK SAEs (width 64, k=4) on PatchCore anomaly residuals of a vision model as an intervention interface. It reports anomaly-detection AUROC and label-effect alignment. It does not measure superposition geometry, capacity, polysemanticity causes, LLM feature spreading, or whether SAE features are canonical units.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that automatically interpreted sparse features give an actionable interface to a frozen detector's anomaly signal. They find MLLM labels align in aggregate with feature effects. They caution that labels are hypotheses and individual SAE features may remain polysemantic.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not reproduce the toy-model method. It applies TopK SAEs to visual anomaly residuals and intervenes on those features for anomaly detection.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports sensitivity to amplification strength, dictionary width and TopK sparsity, MLLM choice, detector, and vision backbone; effects vary across these settings.

fits_no_version.finding: For SAE features of a visual anomaly detector's residuals, features labeled anomaly change scores more on anomalous than normal images under suppression and 2× amplification (pHolm about 2e-6). Distractor-labeled features show no significant class difference.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MLLM-assigned SAE feature labels predict, in aggregate, class-specific causal effects of feature interventions in a vision anomaly detector.

record.problems: No direct evidence on the superposition claims. The authors state that there is no ground-truth annotation for individual SAE features and no guarantee that each interpretation is faithful; their feature-level alignment result is aggregate.
record.rows_left_out: Main AUROC tables and SAE reconstruction-fidelity results are omitted because they evaluate the visual anomaly-detection pipeline rather than the listed superposition claims. Figure 2 reports the feature-level effects retained here.

untested.parts: All parts: toy-model geometry, the sparsity-dependent transition, and near-orthogonal storage.
All parts: capacity competition and dedicated dimensions for important features.
All parts: non-capacity causes of polysemanticity.
All parts. No LLMs are studied. The SAE is trained on vision anomaly residuals and its recoverability is not framed as evidence of superposition.
Completeness, stability and canonicity of SAE features. Tied vs untied variants differ only in dead features, and labels are hypotheses.

record.verdict_notes: Superposition appears only in related work, citing Elhage et al. as a motivation for SAEs. The SAE has width 64 on residuals of dimension d (DINOv3-L features), so it is not overcomplete in a way relevant to superposition. Appendix B reports reconstruction fidelity and width/sparsity sensitivity of the downstream method, which concerns pipeline performance rather than feature canonicity. The MLLM label agreement of 68–81% concerns interpretation, not the features themselves.

versions.untested_parts: Whether sparse features are stored as overlapping, nearly orthogonal directions, and whether there is a sparsity-dependent transition or regular geometry.
Whether polysemanticity results from capacity competition or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure, and whether polysemanticity indicates superposition.
Whether LLM features spread across neurons or sparse features in LLMs can be recovered by a dictionary.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, canonical units of a model's representation.
Whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.
